Augmentation using the FastText model. We participated in three experiments, and it
was found that the combined BERT and FastText approach demonstrated the best
performance.
This research explores the fractions formed by dividing symmetrical and antisymmetrical numbers.

A novel reconstruction model is presented that jointly optimizes CT scan duration, noise levels in detected signals, and material decomposition. The proposed approach minim a specific function that accounts for material accuracy, measurement fidelity, and an L1 penalty term, all while considering a multi-energy CT setup with unknown coefficients and a target object. By sharing a representational space between the original object and energy-specific materials, a variational reconstruction model is adopted. This leads to an optimized object materialization and accurate material decomposition with significantly fewer iterations compared to traditional methods. Corresponding Euler-Lagrange equations and an optimized solver are developed to solve the corresponding material problem. When applied to synthetic data, the approach demonstrates accurate material decomposition and reduces iteration counts by approximately 50% compared to conventional methods like algebraic reconstruction and a previously proposed variational approach, without affecting material accuracy.

Recent advancements in Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) have largely relied on neural network-based methods that require substantial amounts of labeled training data, which is not feasible for numerous historical and minority languages and dialects. To circumvent this limitation, researchers have recently proposed semi-supervised data enhancement techniques that facilitate the creation of synthetic training data from lone document examples. However, this approach is not suitable for HTR due to the inherent characteristics of handwritten text. In response, this research presents a novel technique for creating realistic data for such tasks by breaking down document composition into basic elements and modeling them based on existing literature, before generating artificial text based on these models. Through comprehensive experiments on various languages and dialects, the authors demonstrate that their proposed approach yields superior results, outperforming previous methods using only the generated data for training. The generated data will be publicly available to support further research and development in this area.

Utilizing state-of-the-art nuclear data from SKY3D optical spectroscopy, precise atomic weights were computed for elements up to thulium (atomic number 69) on the standard CIPM scale. A novel pixelated 3D basis function model for the nuclear mean field, paired with an innovative double folding interaction, enabled precise calculations for extremely heavy nuclei, including those up to atomic number 112 and axial atomic masses up to 290. This approach successfully predicted unknown nuclear properties, including those of nucleus $^{293}$112, with remarkable accuracy. Furthermore, the method demonstrated precise calculations for heavy nuclei near the atomic mass limit, labeled "islands of stability," including nuclei near $^{311}$120. Utilizing numerous experimental constraints, a reliable estimate for the nuclear symmetry energy constant was derived and found to be $29.5 \pm 1.1$ MeV.

Quantum systems exhibiting topological characteristics are distinguished from conventional ones by an exceptionally robust protection offered by their properties. Current research heavily employs experimental models, such as the SSH model, to investigate topological quantum phenomena. Despite a current overview of the SSH model's capabilities and limitations existing, a comprehensive analysis remains absent. In this work, we conduct an extensive exploration into various aspects of the SSH model, providing an in-depth examination of the periodic boundary condition and its impact on the system's topological features. To mitigate this impact, we propose implementing a more complex Hamiltonian with multiple sub-lattices. Our research further examines other SSH model elements, including the role of chiral symmetry and the consequences of removing it. We also delve into the significance of band gaps in characterizing topological properties and present an additional approach for their identification. Our comprehensive analysis of characterizations and proposals aim to assist researchers with different backgrounds in navigating the complexities of the SSH model.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators in Bergman spaces associated with certain types of convex domains in $\mathbb{C}^{n-1}$ that possess a common boundary point, as well as composition mappings between these spaces and Berghman spaces of units in the unit ball of $\mathbb{C}^{n-1}$.

We utilized the topological string scale to identify two-loop dual supergravity amplitudes in the anti-de Sitter space and sphere by extending three-loop two-derivative dual supergravity formulas and applying an expansion of the Riemann tensor and its curvature-dependent counterparts. Our results support the n-loop amplitude hypothesis and enable the derivation of two-derivative corrections to type IIB string theory on the sphere with potential implications for string scattering amplitudes in higher dimensions. Furthermore, we found that this corrections preserve the $SO(4, 3)$ symmetry of the self-dual sector on the lightcone and noted that they align exactly with three-loop maximally-helicity-violating amplitudes in $N=4$ super-Yang-Mills theory when expanded in weak anti-de Scription. Our findings also reveal a connection to the gravity/coupling expansion proposal, revealing an unexpected relationship where the proposed loop factors in amplitude are replaced by powers of the anti-de Scription length.

High-performance computing on High-I/O devices is hampered by inefficient memory allocation techniques. In multiple computational fields, including graph analysis and machine learning, the time taken for memory allocation significantly exceeds simulation time on various GPU architectures. Existing solutions, like Hyperbox and the CUDA page-allocation API, often result in 2- to 4-fold improvements; however, they fall short in handling complex data types such as vectors. To address this limitation, we present DynaSOAr, an innovative memory allocation system tailored for high-I/O devices and compatible with object-oriented programming. DynaSOAr leverages pointer analysis, ensures type safety, and employs custom memory managers to optimize memory usage and enhance performance. Our assessments demonstrate DynaSOAr's capability to outperform multiple baseline memory allocation systems by up to 1.8 times in terms of execution time, while reducing execution time variability to less than 10% across various CUDA architectures.

This study explores U(1) model standards that incorporate U(1) gauge symmetry as a combination of U(1)_Y and U(1)_X baryon-lepton symmetry. A list of models that meet specific requirements is provided, and the corresponding model parameters are calculated. Additionally, the model parameters for a lepton universal Z' model in which U(1)' symmetry is broken by a Vev triplet of an SO(10) adjoint 126 representation are determined.

A straw-filled pipe under positive pressure was analyzed using the thin-shell theory 
to examine the stress affecting the fluid flow within the pipe through pressure measurements 
taken along its length while enclosing the soil. Positive longitudinal stress was found in 
the pike area and negative stress in the posterior region. Positive stress contributed to increased 
water yield by facilitating internal fluid movement and pressure buildup. Stresses exceeding 
material strength, measured at 1.1 MPa, can lead to pressurization and hinder nutrient and solid 
matter transport to the pressurized section. Ultimately, this would decrease internal fluid flow and 
result in diminished water yield and increased root stress.

The concept of uncertainty management in machine learning has led to the development of various models, with the Credal Bayesian framework being a prominent example. This framework allows for obtaining guarantees of strength, reflecting the level of confidence in solutions, through probability projections. These projections involve restricting the probability measure to a sub-region defined by specific performance constraints. However, calculating projections can be computationally demanding, particularly when utilizing high-accuracy numerical methods like Mixed-Linear Programming. Our research presents a novel approach to enhance efficiency by formulating strength guarantees and projections as a mixed-integer linear programming problem that can be iteratively restricted using the scenario generation technique. This results in a practical system suitable for real-world applications that we demonstrate on both synthetic data and probablistic reverse time-reduction processes from the oil and gas industry.

We analyze the case of a band insulator in a superfluid Bosonic system under
stochastic lattice modulation, focusing on how the many-body interactions affect
the dynamics. We demonstrate that this influence results in a dissipation of energy
with respect to the band index, causing the system to heat up in a periodic manner.
This phenomenon is comparable to a particle undergoing Bloch oscillations and is
characterized by a predictable relationship between heat and band index. We
estimate the period of heat oscillations based on Gutzwiller's trace formula. To
obtain analytical expressions for the spectrum, we model the scattering between
two non-interacting quasiparticles. This model is valid when thermal energy greatly
exceeds the impact of the band insulator's zone center. A related effect is the
regular emergence of metallic states in certain high-band indices under specific
conditions. Additionally, we provide a qualitative understanding of how the
interaction between quasiparticles impacts the system on a lower heat scale.

A code with neighbour symmetry in a Euclidean space can be defined by a matrix with specific properties. If such a code exists in a Euclidean space with certain characteristics, its corresponding vectors would form a root system with high symmetry. For 3 neighbours, a relationship with quadrangles of specific types can be seen, particularly aligned with types B4, D4, and A5. However, for neighbours greater than 3, any code with such a relationship would have minimal weights either equal to or greater than a specific value. In cases where the code length is odd and neighbour is greater than 4, another high symmetry code with the same weight exists. Codes with minimal weights often relate to dispersion, and codes with a specific property in quadrangles can be found in types A7, D7, and E7.

A 3.4 micron image analysis of the Galactic Centre revealed a massive Sgr A* black hole, which sits at the intersection of a gzbar-shaped region surrounded by dense molecular clouds. Previous studies using a radial density profile method to determine the mass of this area encountered difficulties due to an unknown boundary set by the galactic bulge. This study utilizes a substantial 3.6 micron image to create a 2D correlation function that helps quantify the dense molecular cloud's mass in the region, thereby bypassing the problematic boundary issue. Analysis of 2D correlation functions reveals an elliptical mass distribution with an estimated eccentricity of 0.44. Applying these findings enables an estimation of the massive black hole's mass, which when combined with existing research, suggests a substantial influence on the stable orbit of objects within the CMZ. Additionally, various factors affecting the dense molecular clouds, such as clouds near the black hole, molecular gas along the galactic plane, and the bulge's mass, are analyzed and their contributions assessed. It's concluded that within a specified area around the galactic centre, the dense molecular clouds possess enough mass to influence the stable orbit of objects, while mass within the galactic bulge exerts a stronger gravitational pull, thereby impacting the galactic orbit of objects, such as stars.

We've developed a kinetic model to analyze the temporal evolution of x-ray absorption edges in amorphous and crystalline materials following x-ray pulse excitation. This model accounts for three primary rate constants: ionization, hole capture (recombination), and Auger/hole generation rates. By integrating the model through the x-ray pulse duration, we obtain simulated spectra that can be compared to real-world measurements. These simulations reveal that x-ray absorption spectroscopy serves as an effective probe for tracking electron-hole creation and recombination in complex systems, even when multiple processes occur simultaneously at high ionization rates ($\sim 10^{27}$ s$^{-1}$) and correspondingly short timescales. Furthermore, x-ray absorption spectroscopy's element-specificity enables the study of electron-hole creation and recombination rates associated with specific atomic nuclei. In our investigation, we utilized amorphous and crystalline materials, doped with indium, to demonstrate that x-ray absorption spectroscopy can effectively track electron-hole generation and recombination associated with x-ray induced ionization. Moreover, x-ray absorption spectroscopy enables the study of valence band structures through hole capture at various atomic nuclei, thereby providing insights into valence band compositions through previous electronic structure calculations and known bond configurations. This methodology was demonstrated using the 4f spectra of both amorphous and crystalline materials containing incandescent materials, where analysis through x-ray absorption spectroscopy enabled insight into valence band compositions determined through calculations through hole

Achieving ultra-low-power in digital circuits is a pressing issue due to escalating supply voltages requiring greater than ever before. This challenge stems from varying process parameters affecting digital performance levels. A promising solution involves incorporating greater design flexibility through the incorporation of analog components tailored to specific processes, reducing overall energy consumption significantly, albeit often resulting in diminished reliability. This present work presents an innovative, versatile design strategy employing entirely standard building blocks capable of accurately measuring ambient temperature within a -20{\deg}C to +80{\deg}C range with 0.24{\deg}C resolution,{\deg}C error, and 1.06nJ energy per conversion, and operating at a 500kHz maximum frequency, and functioning across a vast 3.8V voltage range. This solution utilizes basic design elements such as an inverse bias circuit, consistent load divider, and differential amplifier implemented within a fully digital environment utilizing standard 130nm CMOS technology. These building blocks are compatible with diverse process parameters including supply voltages ranging from 0.6V to 1.8V. This robust design can be integrated into various applications, including health monitoring systems, industrial temperature monitoring systems, and even wearable devices, demonstrating its versatility and adaptability.

The projection of a single photon into a entangled state is a key concept in quantum optics and related fields. This process, often associated with the reduction of bright signals, is usually a deterministic outcome resulting from a combination of two specific scenarios - one involving a definite photon emission and another involving the deletion of photons from a state of high photon count. Herein, a form of this phenomenon can be made a choice-dependent, conditional process, effectively allowing for the controlled creation of polarization quantum bits. This is achieved by applying a chosen unitary operation (either rotation or Hadamard) to a high photon count signal (generated through the dilation of a dimer state) and then reducing it to a small photon number outcome via dimer projection. This reduction serves as a reliable indicator for photon entanglement, regardless of the specific unitary operation applied, as demonstrated through both theoretical calculations and experimental findings.

A set of edges in a graph G forms a Euclidean delta-geodetic spanner with delta >= 1 if it preserves all original edges and has at most k edges, while providing approximate shortest paths with length at most delta times the original for every pair of vertices. Our research focuses on creating efficient, virtual Euclidean delta-geodetic spanners, where the set of edges is limited to k = O(n^(1+epsilon)) for any small positive epsilon value. We present a construction method that achieves this, with a specific outcome showing a 4-approximation for delta when epsilon equals 0.1.

Accurate categorization of IoT devices from remote locations is a critical task, yet the use of full device fingerprints is often impractical due to excessive data transfer costs. As a result, researchers have traditionally focused on developing the entire feature set and as this paper argues, it is more efficient to target specific, selected features. We present a novel method, known as CLFS, for calculating cost-aware likelihoods of IoT device types by first determining which features are most useful and then evaluating their transmission costs. The approach leverages a subset of features and adapts probabilistic models like Na\"{i}ve Bayes and Bayesian Networks to specific devices and cost models. Our analysis using a dataset of device fingerprints reveals that CLFS outperforms traditional models, despite considering transmission costs, particularly when communicating with devices at a remote location.

Godel modal logic T extends the basic Herbrand logic with a modal operator that represents topological closure. This paper explores algebraic and relational models for variations of Godel logic that include the modal operator. We focus on a specific extension: logic T with propositional variables, a fixed finite valuations, and a topological Krasnenko-Ceglarz equivalence relation as the underlying topology. We examine the corresponding algebraic structures through the lens of subalgebras of product algebras and their relational models. This study provides a completeness proof for a specific variant of Godel logic with key differences to classical modal logic K.

This research explores leveraging external bilingual data sources for real-time word alignment. It investigates how bilingual data from disparate domains can be utilized to establish word connections across different languages during translation.

This study presents an algorithm for generating a unique solution to Nash equilibria in a game with continuous, smooth payoff functions. It utilizes a distortion rescaling method and is based on the principle of path divergence. The algorithm starts from a pure Nash equilibrium in the game's corner and gradually moves towards the game's interior, converging to a point that satisfies the complementarity conditions and represents a unique Nash equilibrium in the game's interior. We provide several numerical examples, including a game with continuous payoff functions and its corresponding solution computed using the algorithm, as well as an auction model with corresponding parameters and a theoretical example involving an insurer's reinsurance claim.

The theoretical framework of primordial black holes (PBHs) offers a viable solution to multiple dark matter challenges. However, current observations from the gravitational wave detector LIGO and Planck data present obstacles to the standard model of cosmology. In an effort to reconcile these discrepancies, some researchers have proposed the dark PBH model, which uses PBHs to explain dark energy and EVolutions using the code PopSyCLE.

We studied the behavior of wedges made of rigid components at low temperatures, where each consists of four spherical segments arranged in a specific shape - flat on top, and sharply pointed at the bottom. As the space narrowed, these samples naturally formed stately patterns, where their tops aligned perfectly in a lattice structure. Our research delved into the structure at the point where the samples came to a point, where our findings showed an alignment pattern resembling a flower pattern in three dimensions. This was accompanied by a subtle twisting, or "splay," at the point where the samples aligned. The "petals" of this 3D flower pattern pointed in all directions, pointing to possible unique liquid patterns. These patterns could potentially represent three-dimensional patterns with different molecular arrangements.

Recent work on spherical Gaussian processes has resulted in innovative methods for computing lag-spheres distributions and verifying the Markov property for specific random field configurations. Building on this work, we aim to provide more detailed insights into the conditional characteristics of spin systems by defining unique one-step recursions. These recursions will be applied to specific static random field models, including Potts models, Ising-Kac models, and Edwards-Anderson models. We will also explore the influences of long-range interactions in these models, particularly in the context of Ising and ferromagnetic Kac interactions, and we will discuss aspects of phase transitions in these models.

Using a single-pixel detector, we develop a visualization method based on the correlation between a source and a target that doesn't require detecting individual quantum events. Our proposed method utilizes a source based in frequency and an agent with control over polarization, allowing us to formulate a unique figure of merit. We demonstrate the technique experimentally and successfully verify angular correlations with high precision. Since undetected quantum events are processed, the technique benefits from an undestructive measurement property, offering potential for wide-range applications.

Our research shows that the friction in foams is impacted by the arrangement of the liquid within the structure. During the movement of the foam, the local distribution of air and liquid is altered, resulting in the creation of flow patterns that preferentially move liquid through the air structures. This has the effect of increasing the air's relative proportion within the foam. The amount of air within the foam will stay steady after the initial transient period and is directly related to the arrangement of the air's bubbles. The friction coefficient of the foam is composed of two distinct parts, the first of which is independent of the foam's internal structure and the second part is increased as the space available for air within the foam structures increases.

The widespread availability of high-throughput data necessitates advanced techniques for processing class-imbalanced data and detecting anomalous information that conventional methods are incapable of handling effectively. In the fields of genomics and medicine, large-scale, high-throughput studies have become highly time-sensitive and critical, requiring the analysis to be performed within a limited timeframe and critical decision-making to commence promptly on such data. Existing algorithms and deep learning architectures struggle to address these challenges and optimize clinical outcomes. In this research, we present an improved deep learning model that addresses the limitations of existing methods by integrating a modified Batch Normalization layer and the Entropy-Normalized Over Sampling (ENO) approach to enhance the classification performance and outlier identification accuracy of the network. Experimental evaluations on public skin cancer datasets demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed model in handling imbalanced data and achieving accurate classification and anomaly detection. Compared to existing clinical workflows, the novel model exhibits improved sensitivity, precision, recall, F1 score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve metrics. Additionally, the integration of a knowledge graph with the deep learning model facilitates the interpretation of clinical decisions and the identification of knowledge gaps. Fuzzy logic is used to manage uncertainty during the classification process, thereby enhancing the overall transparency and trustworthiness of the decision-making process.

We've carried out a comprehensive study on the electronic properties of sodium using an advanced ab initio approach. Our goal was to examine how quickly electrons lose energy within sodium, which we did by analyzing how their probability changes over time through numerical calculations based on quantum mechanics. Our findings indicate that near the Fermi surface, where electronic interactions are most intense, electrons in sodium tend to remain stable for approximately 10-20 femtoseconds, but in regions farther from this surface, their stability period can extend into the picosecond range. Furthermore, our research provides a dependable foundation for creating simplified models that further investigate how electrons in sodium interact with each other.

In this paper, a novel technique is proposed for simulating phase space using constant-speed Hamiltonian paths to model expansion and contraction processes. Traditional methods for expanding a phase space trajectory often involve rescaling velocities, which can introduce numerical errors due to the varying speeds involved. Our proposed method overcomes this limitation, allowing for a more efficient simulation without artificial scaling. Furthermore, our approach reduces storage requirements and enables a more thorough examination of the phase space during processes such as free expansion, ultimately revealing the truly ergodic components of these systems.

An earlier conjecture proposed that the weights of Kontsevich graphs in his 2007 formula for quantizing symplectic manifolds could be 0, 1, or 2. This initial hypothesis was refined after the discovery that the weights could take negative values. In this theoretical framework, we adapt a previously developed method for determining graph weights by relating them to the connection and curvature of a specific symplectic Poisson structure based on an affine variety defined by the given graph's equations. This approach enables us to prove that the weights are indeed confined to the set of integers and that they strictly fall within the range of -1 to 1 for graphs associated with link embeddings.

We've explored the presence of Naskhaba or Nanoptera in the array structures woodpile and diatomic created using granular materials. These special arrays exhibit unique localized modes, and when minor disturbances occur within a certain frequency range, they produce exponential decay oscillations. This phenomenon is observed in specific configurations: the absence of a gap in the spectrum for the arrangement $\alpha = 0.25$ leads to this decay, whereas small openings facilitate decay with the configuration $\alpha = 0.35$. The study indicates that this decay is due to an interaction between the special array modes and the continuous spectrum of the underlying structure, which occurs regardless of minimal disturbances.

Non-Gaussian correlations cosmic features can offer a glimpse of high-energy phenomena within the early universe.  Some theories propose that these features arise directly from interactions between the inflaton and other fields.  We've found that features can be identified through characteristics in the three-point correlation function of specific multipoles which we've generalized to higher n-point correlations.  Our research indicates that these features exhibit distinct patterns characterized by an 'infrared enhancement', 'on-shell pole structure', and specific prism features that become apparent when certain multipoles are examined.  These characteristics serve as distinct markers of the early universe's inflaton dynamics and can be detected even if features themselves are suppressed.

We introduce a new class of graphs called accordion graphs and provide a systematic method to determine all cyclic permutations of vertices that result in isomorphisms between accordion graphs and the square of their catheter graphs. This knowledge enables us to easily enumerate and identify all isomorphism classes of small accordion graphs by utilizing a pairing of edges that avoids cliques of size two, which we also completely classify. Furthermore, this isomorphism square of the catheter is shown to be the smallest known example of an asymmetric quartic vertex-transitive graph for a non-trivial case.

In quantum walking, two key dynamics principles govern the evolution of the system: globally balanced and locally constrained. The balanced principle relates to balanced growth rates and stable distribution patterns, while the constrained principle connects to power-law behaviors in these systems. These dynamics principles apply not only to complex systems but also to quantum walking algorithms. The balanced principle in quantum walking manifests as a separation between the primary and secondary components of the system's amplitude, leading to a stable, balanced state in the system's probability distribution. The constrained principle in quantum walking refers to the behavior of its amplitude that determines its global and local states globally and locally, respectively. The constraints on the behavior of its global and local states determine whether they exhibit exponential or power-law behaviors, respectively. This research investigates the effectiveness of vision transformer architecture for self-supervised learning tasks, aiming to understand the mechanisms driving its success. The study highlights a limitation in existing research that treats transformer components as immutable and beyond design considerations. In addressing this issue, the authors present a practical approach for enhancing transformers by incorporating the positional information considerator (TAP), which compensates for the lack of inherent spatial structure translation symmetry in the architecture. Additionally, the authors develop a novel transformer design that relies on non-parametric non-data dependent memory operations, eliminating the need for redundant computational steps and reducing the computational load associated with self-supervised training. As a result, the proposed TAP and novel memory-based memory attention (MaM) architecture show improved performance, achieving comparable or better results than existing leading techniques such as Barlows Twins and DNCC in 20% and 1% data regimes on the ImageNet-21k benchmark.

A researcher has proposed an all-encompassing dissipation dark matter model, which directly relates the flux of energy and momentum. By integrating this model into the framework of gravitational field equations in a homogeneous and isotropic universe, several mathematical formulas have been established to describe the evolution of energy density and Hubble parameter. These equations facilitate various fluid models, particularly those of combined type, in an attempt to provide an overall understanding of the underlying structure of the universe's matter content and its associated energy flows. Research indicates that a combination of two types of dark matter within a single fluid model with outgoing energy can accurately represent a universe in a matter-radius system that is stable and gradually transitions to a radiative equilibrium. Furthermore, analytical solutions have been developed to study a combined dark matter model consisting of a viscous dust component and a dotted fluid containing outgoing energy, in an effort to assess the impact of energy leakage on the dynamics of the universe's evolution. Research results suggest that such a universe remains dynamically stable across the entire timeline, regardless of energy exchange between its components, which is applicable to a broad range of cosmological contexts.

A simple direct proof of a theorem stating the invariance of certain function spaces under solutions of the incompressible Euler equations in n dimensions for n greater than or equal to 2 in a specific mathematical context involving trigonometric norms and coefficients. This proof utilizes a counterexample that was originally formulated by Cartmell, incorporating modifications suggested by Chae and Kim, to establish the invariance failure of these spaces. Additionally, an alternative explanation for a pre-existing proof of invariance failure for incompressible Euler equations in three dimensions was presented, involving the incorporation of a small perturbation in the initial data and trigonometric norms and coefficients.

Recent advances in text-to-image generation through diffusion models have been impressive, but achieving complete image fidelity remains a challenge, as fully controlling the creation process proves difficult. To overcome this limitation, we aim to guide the semantic aspect of generation, thereby reducing the complexity of guiding the diffusion process itself. Employing multiple curves in the diffusion process generates multiple 'steams', thereby facilitating slower and more controlled creation. Our proposed method utilizes these steams, enabling parallelism and allowing for multiple external creators to guide the generation simultaneously within the diffusion latent space. Our experimental results confirm that our method yields superior performance compared to prevailing techniques, particularly in achieving alignment between image content and user demands.

A novel Bayesian approach to a reversible data hiding scheme is presented, focusing on extracting hidden data from image sequences using neural networks. A key advantage of this method is its ability to minimize the distortion of the carrier, resulting in higher payload capacities. Initially, an in-place reversible concealment method is applied to individual frames, followed by the use of a dehosting network to remove residual artifacts and optimize performance for subsequent frames. Since the ANN-based methods are problem-specific and lack generalizability, a high-performance capability is demonstrated on sequences on a test platform, including the Lena video and the Star Wars video.

This letter investigates the possibility that J/psi decays into invisible particles by utilizing the J/psi electronic structure effective field theory. If neutrinos possess non-zero masses, J/psi can split into a photon and one neutrino-antineutrino pair if energy-momentum conservation is respected. If J/psi comprises not only neutrinos but also dark energy components governed by a universal effective field theory constant G_0, J/psi can spontaneously decay. By applying the precision measurements of radiative and invisible J/psi decays, we establish constraints applicable to a broader cosmological scale, yielding two overarching constants that define both neutrino mass limits and the maximum density of dark energy.

Two distinct magnetic peak observations in the solar atmosphere indicate the presence of bright spots at active regions. artifacts, the NCKM model, both suggest a dual-natured magnetic field configuration.  To verify this theoretical model observationally, we performed spectral line analysis in the Na I D doublet range.  By utilizing the SOHO/SUMI telescope, we discovered significant differences in intensity and temperature between bright spots and the surrounding solar atmosphere.  Our findings indicate a lower temperature in the spot area, lower temperature in the spot area, lower pressure in the spot area, lower pressure in the spot area, a temperature difference of about 500K between the spot area and the surrounding area.  These results validate the magnetic field model in the region of interest.  By comparing the magnetic field model to other data sources, we have further confirmed this model's accuracy.  We have also found a substantial difference in the temperature structure of the spot area and the surrounding area.  These results validate the magnetic field model in the region of interest.  By comparing the magnetic field model to other data sources, we have further confirmed this model's accuracy.

In human perception, identifying objects and their properties from moving situations is a crucial skill that enables us to predict and control movement. Recent breakthroughs in technology, using neural networks, have also achieved remarkable success in this area. However, the connection between how humans and AI identify moving objects is still unclear. To explore this connection, an experiment was conducted where both humans and AI were tested on the same moving object recognition task. The key finding is that there's a strong correlation between these performances, and interestingly, both tend to perform worse as the objects start moving. What's more, when presented with very brief video clips, both humans and AI perform at their peak accuracy.

If cosmic magnetic fields existed before the Big Bang, it's possible that their current forms are actually shadows of their original self. We propose a theory where a new type of dark matter interacts with these magnetic fields, reflecting them instead of creating them. This dark matter is composed of stable particles that carry a unique spin and interaction with the magnetic field through a seemingly unexpected interaction. Although the properties of these particles are physically restricted in four dimensions, they can exist in higher dimensional spaces. The existence of these magnetic field particles can be detected by existing instruments at the Large Hadron Collider if they have masses under 1 GeV, or by astronomical observations if they interact in outer space.

Extreme climate events pose significant threats to the environment and human society, necessitating the integration of various models into a data-driven framework for enhanced prediction capabilities. Despite the success of large language models (LLMs) in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP), the potential of these models for climate prediction has yet to be thoroughly explored due to the increasing challenges posed by the length of climate time series data. This research presents a innovative solution, the Climate Action Transformer (CAT), designed specifically for effective climate prediction, which overcomes the limitations associated with the very large model and annotation costs. Unlike traditional climate prediction models that may struggle with capturing long-range dependencies due to reliance on local patterns, the CAT model excels in the classification and regression tasks related to the Australian forest fire danger index. By introducing a new cross-attention mechanism that combines spatial and temporal information through a shifting window approach, CAT ensures that the model can learn essential essential features while maintaining a manageable model size and training cost, thereby providing a robust foundation for accurate climate predictions. Furthermore, the enhanced long-range dependency learning capability of CAT contributes significantly to the model's overall performance.

A model of three dark matter particles based on the $S_3$ symmetry of the three-Higgs-doublet model is investigated, with dark matter particles interacting through various mediators, including physical CP-odd and charged scalar particles, as well as physical CP-odd and charged pseudoscalar particles. Various constraints on these models, imposed by the relic density, direct and indirect dark matter searches, and electroweak precision measurements, are examined in a range of parameter space. Scenarios where one or two dark matter particles are predominantly present are analyzed using both exact $S_3$ symmetry and approximate $S_3$-like symmetry. While models with dark dark matter particles interacting via scalar particles are difficult to accommodate the relic density across the full parameter space, those with dark dark matter particles approximately interacting with pseudoscalar particles largely comply with all relevant constraints.

A proposed ppt quaternary assumption posits that any four qubit systems composed of pure ppt states, where the transition from one system to another forms a non-intersecting grid, should result in at least one of the systems lacking a separable breakdown into individual components. We are poised to disprove this assumption by presenting a particular ppt state that is inherently quadrantized in the context of the first two systems and the combined third and fourth systems, representing a state of complete mutual orthogonality across all four systems. Furthermore, we can extend this ppt state to encompass all four systems as individual parts, thereby achieving total quadrantization. Notably, a specific instance using isotropic states is also included in our analysis.

Neural signal transmission is limited by various factors such as axonal length, action potential voltage amplitude and duration, and synaptic congestion. These consequences stem from ions entering and leaving the axon, causing ions to accumulate and the intracellular environment becoming acidic. To address these issues, four regulatory mechanisms have been identified: ion channel adaptation, buffer systems, transporters, and active pumps. Existing models can only simulate one of these mechanisms at a time, while our innovative approach uses simultaneous feedback optimization to model all four. Our work validates the biological plausibility of our approach through successful simulations of sodium-potassium-pumps, as well as simulations predicting the effects of Alzheimer's disease and global cooling on neuronal function.

The analysis of complex systems like financial data often benefits from the use of network science. This research employs the use of network motifs to investigate a set of 3000, 10000 and 50000 date-stamped stock prices as an experiment, selecting 5000 randomly assigned initial assets in conjunction with dynamically added comparable assets at regular intervals. The study's results reveal that distinct price evolution patterns yield unique network structures, encompassing various network motif composition ratios. Additionally, the research indicates that higher frequency networks are associated with real-world data and that a model utilizing a mean-reversion process successfully replicates the characteristics of real-world data, while another model utilizing a random walk process fails to replicate these characteristics.

As a star loses its surrounding material and consequently loses mass, it triggers the collapse of a surrounding disk and emits intense radiation as it transforms into a black hole. A recent study has assessed the properties of the resulting emissions for a specific type of collapse, where a white dwarf star collapses directly into a black hole. It discovers that the shape of the final black hole's event horizon is distorted due to the presence of the dense stellar remnant, which significantly affects the properties of the emitted gravitational waves. Furthermore, simulations have shown that the emitted radiation follows a power-law pattern and the system emits a burst of electromagnetic radiation that peaks around the time the white dwarf reaches the center of its orbit and then decays exponentially following the collapse. It is suggested that this type of collapse and emission process may be more common than previously thought.

We begin by establishing the fundamental three-body waveform and its associated baryonic currents in a general framework to describe $\tau$-lepton semileptonic three-body decays. This enables a precise representation of form factors in terms of invariant masses within the three-body system. Our analysis also includes an in-depth discussion on the calculation methods for form factors, incorporating both theoretical and experimental data. Furthermore, we outline a comprehensive format for three-body decay matrix elements and present a theoretical model based on light-cone sum rules. This model primarily focuses on light mesons but can be extended to heavier semihadronic states via light-cone QCD sum rules. Ultimately, our work serves as a foundational reference for an in-depth study of three-body $\tau$ decays.

The study of parametrized similarity metrics, such as the Tversky distance introduced in 1973, has been overlooked in information theory despite its widespread use in various fields. The distance measures the differences between two sets of items, taking into account their sizes and overlapping elements. The study presents a comprehensive analysis of the distance by comparing it to the normalized information distance and exploring the topological properties of the associated space as the weights of different factors change.

Improving low-quality images affected by motion blur is a crucial task in visual restoration. Although the problem of single image deblurring for rigid objects is relatively well-studied, extending solution frameworks to non-rigid objects remains challenging. This difficulty stems from the intricate relationship between the original image and its motion blur version, compounded by the difficulty in accurately estimating movement. In this research, we focus on the complex deblurring problem applicable to human and scene images, considering the interplay of human expressions and environmental dynamics. Utilizing the recent advances in image super-resolution, we develop a practical pseudo-blur generator that produces realistic blur based on original image features, thereby facilitating the training of a deep denoising network. This approach enables the deblurring of feature-rich images highlighting human facial expressions and environmental details. Our method's effectiveness is validated through comparative analysis of the restored images in terms of visual quality and the accurate reconstruction of the original images.

Inspired by nature's design, where neurons learn through adaptive connections, our innovative approach utilizes adaptive DNA base-pairing as artificial synapses that can learn and recall patterns at the molecular level, eliminating the need for external assistance. One key benefit of this molecular framework is its ability to self-assemble completely on its own. Through a universal adaptation of the DNA-WIS algorithm, our system replicates the behavior of standard neural networks by capturing input data and performing calculations based on the framework's density and topological structure. Furthermore, our research explores the potential applications of this adaptive framework in solving complex mathematical and biological problems, including the reconstruction of DNA sequences and protein folding predictions that defy traditional prediction methods.

A specific type of completeness in ultrapowers of ordered sets has been investigated in the context of nonarchimedanically complete intervals. This study provides a characterization of such completeness through finite interval sequences and demonstrates that certain properties of ordered sets are necessary for this completeness to hold in their ultrapowers. Additionally, the study examines how these properties are preserved under the ultrapower operation when these sets have a maximum element and how certain properties are related to one another. Furthermore, the study presents a characterization of bounded completeness in linear sets with a defined convergence concept and establishes connections to other types of completeness with maximum elements.

We are at a point where machine learning models are being evaluated based on
outstanding achievements in benchmark suites. Nevertheless, it is crucial to
acknowledge that any given model may be influenced by several benchmarks in
unexpected and often unintended ways. A potential risk arises from the fact that
some benchmarks may inadvertently skew a model's performance due to hidden
cues, thus limiting its generalizability to other scenarios. The question
remains as to whether current evaluation protocols are sufficient in detecting
such issues. This work presents an evaluation of big-bench models using
multiple benchmarks, examining both their convergence towards optimal results
and their susceptibility to hidden cues. Our investigation reveals that the
employement of dataset particular profiling offers a more thorough and
comprehensive evaluation protocol compared to traditional evaluation methods.
Using this protocol, we identified several problems that appear to be solved
primarily through the reliance on hidden cues, highlighting the importance of
further research and development in this area. Additionally, we propose the
integration of this evaluation protocol into the machine learning research
community to provide a clearer picture of a model's true capabilities and
limitations.

A graph can be colored using at most k colors, where each color is assigned to a separate set of vertices that form an independent set. Furthermore, a graph must contain a complete subgraph with k vertices. Reinforcing the classic graph 4-color theorem, it can be proven that if a graph has at least k squares and is not requiring more than 4 colors, it must allow for a proper coloring where each monochromatic set contains at least one square. Similarly, if a graph has at least (k-1) pentagons and uses fewer than 5 colors, it can be properly colored at a vertex level where each group forms a cycle. We also investigate the minimum number of specific shapes, such as quadrilaterals and pentagons, a graph needs to avoid rising to the next color. We establish lower bounds on these numbers and propose hypotheses regarding these values' exactness. Lastly, it is proven that adding edges within squares or pentagons adds at least one square or pentagon to the resulting graph if it maintains its original chromatic number.

This study proposes an adaptable correntropy-induced distance (CID) based graph signal restoration (GSR) method, referred to as Sturdy Correntropy-Induced Error Based Graph Signal Restoration with a Kernel Width Optimization (SCIE-BGSRWO). Traditional GSR methods utilizing data fidelity measure (DFM) based on the least-squares (LS) principle have certain limitations including low resistance to outliers and noise. To address this, SCIE-BGSRWO replaces LS with a novel optimized correntropy-based penalty that utilizes the可变 kernel width optimization (KWO) technique, which adjusts the kernel bandwidth automatically during iteration for each residue. To enhance the robustness of this method, it is combined with a block coordinate descent (BCD) algorithm that iteratively optimizes the sparse error and the signal via the least-laplace approximation and the correntropy-based penalty, respectively. Furthermore, this method can be applied to various noise types. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that this method outperforms existing GSR methods.

In our investigation, we introduce a method to create interference patterns using an entangled mixture of atoms with different spin states, and our proposed state of the art input successfully exceeds the interference pattern's detection limits of a leading interference detector. A proposed experiment using rubidium-87785 MHz spinor atoms will demonstrate the effectiveness of our state creation method using a technique called stimulated interference, and our findings show that our generated interference patterns exceed the detector's noise barriers. Furthermore, we introduce methods to verify the quality of the created interference patterns and calculate the required atom counts for successful experiments.

We examine the initial eigenvalue problem $\Delta u + \lambda u = 0$ under the influence of a nonlinear Robin boundary condition, specifically $-\frac{\partial u}{\partial n} = |u|^{p-1}u$ for $u>\epsilon$, where $1<p<3$. Here $\epsilon$ is a very small positive number. Our objective is to determine the asymptotic behavior of the initial eigenvalue $\lambda_1(\epsilon)$ as $\epsilon$ approaches zero. This is achieved by making precise estimates of the problem's ground state. Our findings in this work extend the eigenvalue estimates of Berestycki, Coffman and Ni's earlier research.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) play a crucial role in processing data that's structured as a graph. A typical GCNN process involves transforming input data through a series of graph convolution operations, each incorporating parameters that enable the network to learn and understand relationships within data that's either unstructured or has a specific structure. A recurring, straightforward approach in GCNNs corresponds to matching filters, which are often used as a standard method to analyze and comprehend the structural characteristics of data. Nevertheless, this conventional method faces a significant issue as it fails to adequately capture the complex, non-linear relationships within and between unstructured and structured data. This paper seeks to bridge this gap to bring clarity and understanding to graph convolution operations, by utilizing the matched filter approach to reveal the fundamental connections between data's structured and unstructured aspects and their relevance to analysis. Furthermore, this paper offers a mathematical framework to predict the performance of the matched filter method by formulating and analyzing the optimization problems it represents.

The rise of Generative AI has significantly transformed the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP), particularly in the area of dependency analysis. Despite the progress made by previous models, they often require substantial annotation and can be overly influenced by syntactic features, which may not fully capture the essential characteristics of Dependency Parsing. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel framework called Deep Contextualized Auto-training (DCAT) for low-resource Dependency Analysis. This framework leverages a pre-trained language model, which is then fine-tuned through automated transformation that preserves the essential information of a parsing syntax while eliminating the label requirements. We thoroughly examine various design choices of DCAT and compare our results with state-of-the-art models across multiple datasets, yielding superior performance in most cases and achieving significant computational efficiency by reducing the need for annotated data by over 90%. Notably, the approach can also enhance pre-trained language models' performance in Dependency Analysis tasks. Our research and code are freely accessible at the given link.

We've completed our study of the $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ transition form factors using the light-front duality method and found excellent agreement with both lattice QCD and light-front TMD calculations. Furthermore, this framework yields a value for the $|V_{cb}|$ parameter that is consistent with other measurements and has a relatively small error margin of 3.5 percent.

Our research expands the application of membrane methods to incorporate non-obvious symmetry relationships. Initially, we explored how symmetry relationships can exist without being immediately apparent and found that they can be captured using membrane computations. We then extended the framework to include parallel symmetry relationships between multiple groups of Turing machines, and demonstrated its effectiveness by analyzing the equivalence of Type 2 Grammars and Vector Grammars. Our work also paves the way for the definition of n-membrnes systems, where multiple symmetry relationships exist between groups of Turing machines across multiple membranes.

A new variation of the P time model is developed by modifying the conventional model to remove a constraint on polynomial size, specifically by replacing it with a size limit function l(p) that remains subexponential. The removed constraint was the polynomial size limit on networks, which has been reinstated in this new model. Despite this change, it is proven that the two model differences do not affect problems in P, even when one of these differences is removed. Moreover, an extension of this proof shows that any problem solvable in non-deterministic log time can be solved using a network of the specified subexponential size and is equivalent to problems containing a Cai-Furer-Immerman graph as a local subgraph.

Research has shown that substituting Bi for Eu in (Eu_1-xBi_x)2Ir2O7 significantly raises the Mott transition temperature. We performed HAXPES studies on (Eu_1-xBi_x)2Ir2O7 where the composition ranged from x = 0.1 to 09. The measurements revealed increased Bi 5d character in the valence band as the Bi concentration increased, alongside increased Ir 5d band width. Notably, samples with x >= 0.5 exhibited an increase in Ir 5d band width and valence electron count, exceeding requirements for electron count associated with an insulating state, yielding electron counts above 5/e cell. These measurements align with theoretical predictions and the observed metal-insulator transition behavior in these materials. The study also found increased hybridization between Bi 5d and Ir 5d orbitals as the Bi composition increased, suggesting this coupling influences the electron count and may cause electron localization. Ultimately, the study concludes increased Bi-Ir hybridization may destabilize the insulating phase.

This monograph introduces an innovative concept for exploring two-dimensional value function properties. It focuses on a novel essence mapping for value functions, defining a comprehensive criterion for its existence. By introducing this criterion, numerous useful characteristics of the essence mapping become accessible. It supports efficient two-dimensional Lipschitz selections and provides high-quality approximations for function values. It possesses substantial benefits compared to existing selection methods, particularly in terms of approximate solution efficiency. The monograph presents a versatile method for selection and demonstrates its effectiveness through various case studies. It offers a novel perspective on value function properties and provides a useful tool for further research in two-dimensional set-valued mappings.

Building on Eichler, Sch\'e\'e, and Verheul's research, we explore circular data such as direction, angle, and orientation. Connectionist models and decision tree algorithms often represent this type of data using a circle or by choosing between a value and its negation. Consequently, the prediction output can be turn, point, or up-down, necessitating the evaluation of the relationship between noise and loss functions under these representations. We show the equivalence of these models through their loss functions' behavior, also addressing nontransitive losses where relation A > B does not always imply B > A due to local fluctuations in performance. Using real-world datasets related to neural networks, we provide concrete examples of nontransitive losses.

Recent advancements in cross-platform setup compilers have shown significant potential to enhance software flexibility by allowing modifications with minimal re-compilation overhead, however this setup space often suffers from being 'fat' due to unnecessary code remnants. Eliminating 'fat' remains an open challenge as it involves intricate analysis to pinpoint, evaluate, and optimize the removed code. We conducted a comprehensive investigation on 'fat' elimination through our developed tool, DropDropDrop, which comprehensively analyses a program's execution during runtime and identifies code remnants. Based on the analysis results, DropDropDrop recompiles the original program, removing the identified 'fat' during specific setup configurations, thereby enhancing the program's flexibility and resource efficiency. DropDropDrop successfully reduced the size of 14 open-source projects by up to 44%, with top performances achieved in projects jackson-databind (71%), rebar3 (62%), and gaia (58%), while specifically targeting and eliminating 'fat' in specific gauges for rebar3 (42%) and gaia (80%).

We suggest a new method for detecting sub-GeV dark matter that relies on a novel process from nuclear interactions, and can be implemented using either a liquid or solid argon detector. This method differs from the standard one by identifying the total number of emitted electrons rather than just those produced by the interaction's initial point, which significantly reduces background noise. A simulated experiment with an assumed 100 argon atoms and 256 days of operation indicates that this method could confirm the existence of dark matter particles weighing between 100 MeV and 10 GeV at approximately three statistical deviations above the background.

The overall evolution of both the J-C model and its opposite, the anti-JC model, along with an input field, are studied using a combination of mathematical techniques including differential equations and infinite series expansions. As a result, precise expressions for the state of the system are achieved, enabling the analysis of two key phenomena: (1) dynamics, particularly how a maximum entanglement is reached and influenced by different system parameters; and (2 transmission characteristics, including an interesting absorption behavior observed in the anti-JC model due to an infinitely repeated process of absorption and emission).

Heart rate (HR) is a vital physiological indicator reflecting the balance of autonomic nervous system activities and the body's overall physiological state. Assess the heart rate variability (HRV), using several established features, as a reliable method to diagnose conditions such as depression and anxiety and to evaluate recovery levels of high-performance athletes. Effective assessment of the autonomic nervous system and identification of arrhythmias also depend on accurate HR measurement. Nurses and healthcare professionals can use HRV analysis to provide tailored biofeedback, including interventions like appropriate workload and rest periods. Precise assessment of the autonomic nervous system and the detection of abnormal patterns in HR data require accurate time-stamped HR readings. Traditional methods of HR measurement and analysis often fall short due to the noisy and irregular nature of current techniques. In contrast, the proposed research presents an advanced approach to measuring HR, focusing on capturing its apparent frequency and patterns in real-time video footage and accurately determining the autonomic nervous system's response. The research utilizes a novel technique based on advanced deep learning algorithms and carefully selected data sets, using ECG recordings as the ground truth for validation and evaluation. The research compares the proposed method to existing techniques and demonstrates the effectiveness of the approach in various applications and scenarios.

A cooperative and equilibrium-based model, the active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, equates human memory and velocity fluctuation. This process arises from a function, however, it creates challenges as the position autocorrelation and diffusion behavior diverge from real-world data. This study investigates these discrepancies by exploring the impact of integrated active work in the AOP model, along with alternative representations of the active force's mean and variance. The cooperative work derived in this work enables examination of the system's response to active forces and explores the relationship between derived work distributions and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. The study reveals how varying mean and variance affect the system's dynamics, ultimately equating explored space and time-averaged occupation times. The authors' modeling choices offer possibilities to tune and fit the system's derived quantities.

This study presents HUMBI, a vast multiview dataset comprising 1.33 million carefully annotated human body gesture sequences. Each view in HUMBI features 2D joint skeletons, and we incorporate two novel benchmarks: joint detection and body pose estimation, consciously avoiding the use of explicit garment cues. HUMBI's novel approaches effectively tackle garment ambiguity and occlusion, offering a valuable resource for research on human body pose estimation. Our research on these two tasks outperforms existing state-of-the-art datasets by significant margins, and we extoll the value of HUMBI's large-scale nature and diverse scenarios in fostering research breakthroughs in joint detection and body pose estimation.

Despite the success of multilingual pre-trained transformers in NLP tasks, they often struggle with language-specific adaptations and can be costly to retrain. This paper presents a set of interventions to enhance the cross-lingual transfer ability of these models without extensive retraining. A novel representation learning approach, forming the basis of our method, involves creating a task representation for each input that captures the target model's output. We employ this multilingual task representation as a weak supervision signal to guide the model's output, effectively aligning its cross-lingual task spaces. This method, combined with other strategies such as increasing the target language's data or utilizing parent language data, offers promising results. We validate our proposal through experiments on sentiment analysis and production prediction tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method in enhancing cross-lingual performance.

A limited amount of high-resolution information in low-resolution video sequences hinders the accuracy of image predictions.  Current state-of-the-art methods like BasicVSR, which is a leading video super-resolution technique, effectively propagates temporal contexts but suffers from blurry image predictions due to in accurate frame alignment and motion estimation.  By addressing these issues, this study enhances BasicVSR by propagating high-resolution foreground-labeled pairs through spatial attention and a multi-scale residual learning framework.  Additionally, the study develops an aligned feature map to improve the accuracy of motion estimation and frame alignment within the network.  Experimental evaluation on multiple datasets demonstrates the proposed method outperforms BasicVSR, producing superior results in terms of visual quality and video restoration consistency.  Quantitative results also confirm the proposed method surpasses the aligned feature map's effectiveness in promoting temporal consistency and accuracy.

In multi-task learning, the simultaneous execution of several tasks can improve sample efficiency and versatility, yet it poses challenges in avoiding model overwrites and inefficiencies due to common patterns. Model-based approaches to multi-task reinforcement learning have been developed and enhanced using destructive interference, but they struggle with stability and generalizability due to the models' vulnerability to rewards and unpredictable changes during training, leading to poor performance. We explore three key characteristics that affect models in multi-task learning and introduce a framework designed to develop robust models and create models tailored to specific tasks automatically. The framework's components serve as safeguards that mitigate issues and optimize models without requiring additional computation, focusing on ensuring models' consistency, preventing them from failing, and disabling them when they become ineffective across tasks. Through theoretical analysis and experiments on diverse models and tasks, we demonstrate the value of this framework in enhancing models' capacity to operate in multiple tasks and demonstrate the practical applications of our framework on existing multi-task reinforcement learning models.

A class of heat engines with a finite number of states that operate in perfect synchronization with the finite time it takes for them to change states has been studied. Under specific constraints, where the sole limitation is the finite number of states they can occupy, these engines have an optimal configuration. Notably, this model converges to a well-known engine design as the number of states increases significantly. Furthermore, by applying an specific restriction, where the engine's states are evenly spaced, numerous engines with optimal configurations can be created. Each of these designs has distinct characteristics and a unique mathematical formula for their efficiency. A detailed analysis of these results includes extensive comparisons of their performance.

Future developments in solar and wind energy technologies are expected to significantly contribute to meeting global energy needs. A comprehensive evaluation of their vulnerability to the adverse effects of extreme weather events, such as hurricanes and storm surges, along with underlying uncertainties, is crucial. These uncertainties stem from factors including energy system layout and capacity, model intricacies, and data accuracy. To address these challenges, we have developed a sophisticated modeling framework that considers the geographical distribution, temporal progression, and interplay of storm events and secondary effects like energy shortages and power outages. Based on this model, we calculate probability-based metrics to assess energy system reliability and resilience in a quantifiable manner. Utilizing real-world data from 2005's New Orleans Hurricane Katrina, we demonstrate how our model facilitates the analysis and monitoring of energy systems under various scenarios.

This paper develops the Dirac operator theory within the framework of Clifford analysis. A key finding of this study is the demonstration that any monogenic polynomial of degree n can be expressed as a sum of specific homogeneous components. Furthermore, the paper outlines the structure of a general solution to the Dirac equation in terms of Clifford series. Using this framework, the paper specifically examines the Laplace equation and monogenic functions, and further investigates the theory of eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator. A central finding of this study is the proof that a continuous function on the unit <think>-overline{R}^{m+1} sphere is the uniform limit on the unit sphere of its Taylor series expansions within the unit ball. As a direct consequence, the paper specifically examines the theory of eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator. Some key findings include the proof that a continuous function on the unit 3-overline{R}^{m} sphere is the uniform limit on the unit sphere of its Taylor series expansions within the unit ball and the proof that a continuous function on the unit 3-overline{R}^{m} sphere is the uniform limit on the unit sphere of its Taylor series expansions within the unit ball.

We use Baker diagrams to analyze countable hypermorphic systems like the Dyck system of Chacon. 
For the $n$-level Dyck system, we identify $n$-level heterochaos equivalence to a specific countable shift space $\Sigma_{n,2}$ and a specific measure $\mu_{n,2}$. 
We observe that $\mu_{2,2}$ aligns with the maximal entropy measure in the $n=2$ level of the Dyck system. 
However, for $n>2$, the $\mu_{n,2}$ measure in the $n$-level Dyck system isn't the maximal entropy measure. 
This discrepancy, a first finding, suggests a possible mechanism for the 'failure of the entropy approachability theorem' identified by Glasner and Tanaki.

This research explores enhanced scalar production in collider experiments and the potential these scenarios offer for discovering new particles. We consider the mediating role of vector-like quarks in scalar couplings to the Higgs and a third-generation of extended fermions. Enhancing couplings can significantly increase production rates at colliders like the Large Hadron Collider (HLLHC) and the Future Circular Collider (FcCc), the muon collider (mcEc), and the SuperB factory. These cases involve scalars that can decay into a Higgs boson and heavy charged particles, enabling rich final states that can be produced with high rates. Even when enhanced couplings result in suppressed production, the large branching ratios of decays may still produce observable muon–electron and lepton pair states. We conclude that enhanced scalar production or its decays provide rich muon potential for discovering new physics at upcoming colliders and even in the context of the Standard Model. We also perform an enhanced scalar production analysis at the HLLhc and mcEc colliders.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) designed to synthesize speech. PwNet is an improved version of the existing waveguide neural network model, WaveNet. It incorporates a pitch-aware dilated convolution neural network (DCNN) into Wvn's front-end to produce better speech synthesis quality, particularly in terms of formant structure and periodicity. The incorporation of this module enables the model to learn speech dynamics at the level of the original waveform while also capturing the periodic nature of the signal. As a result, QPnet outperforms the existing models in the speech synthesis evaluation benchmarks.

The growing popularity of digital content has led to an overwhelming amount of choice, with users facing the paralyzing effect because they're unable to make informed choices. This issue's solution lies in filtering and recommending the most suitable content based on user preferences. Traditional collaborative filtering systems face limitations in tackling the problems of distant user tastes and information scarcity. This research puts forth an innovative cooperative filtering method grounded in biclustering and user profiles to resolve these challenges. The proposed approach employs biclustering to group user behaviors and overfit prevention, with each user then using their unique preferences to identify local clusters and provide recommendations. The suggested framework's performance is tested with real-world datasets, demonstrating its superior capacity for accuracy and handling varying user tastes compared to state-of-the-art collaborative filtering models.

Precise knowledge of the sun's activity and its properties is extremely important for understanding the disk-integrated HARPS-N solar activity index's behavior. By creating a detailed database of sunspot observations from the National Observatory of Madrid between 2018 and 2019, we were able to analyze the spectral regions most affected by activity. This was done by examining the equivalent widths of specific iron lines in those regions. We then compared the data to the Harris Activity Index and found that certain spectral regions have more variable behavior, which has important implications for using the HARPS-N activity index as an exoplanet activity index. We propose new markers to improve its accuracy and suggest that the HARPS-N activity index should be recalibrated or that new spectral regions should be considered for its computation.

Recent research on topological superconductivity has produced significant advancements, particularly in identifying an 0-bias peak in Josephson junctions containing Kondo lattice nanowires which may be indicative of non-Abelian Majorana fermions. Although various experiments have been conducted to confirm its existence, a definitive conclusion remains elusive due to noise and confusion with other types of peaks. To address this problem, our proposal suggests utilizing tunneling spectroscopy with an Ohmic damping regime by employing resistive electrodes in junctions to eliminate noise and distinguish the Majorana peak from other types of peaks.

In the context of higher category theory, there is a functor that associates each bicategorical localization with its corresponding fully bicategorical localization, effectively tracking these transformations. Not all localizations are effective; for instance, certain categories like commutative comonads have a localized version that fails to become effective. A key question arises: under what conditions does a localized category effectively become the target of this transformation? A solution to this query is achieved by characterizing effective localizations as those possessing specific characteristics: their localization functors have both a left and a right adjoint, which together establish an equivalence between the original and modified categories. These conditions can also be interpreted through the lens of topoi and localizations.

Recent breakthroughs in deep neural networks have made it possible to extract artistic style from various images and apply them to other images, effectively achieving style transfer. Conventionally, this process involves a network trained to minimize the difference between the output and a desired target image, with the style transfer occurring during the training with pre-trained image representations. However, this traditional approach has several limitations, such as the inapplicability to high-resolution images and the need for a large amount of data. Moreover, it cannot handle cases where the target image is not available, such as when performing a tone mapping. A new approach is presented here that overcomes these drawbacks by utilizing pairs of images and extracting style through pixel-level correspondence. The proposed method employs a regression network that regresses the corresponding high-resolution feature maps or low-level image components of the pair, allowing for a more accurate style transfer and tone mapping. The method's capabilities are demonstrated through successful results on both low-resolution style transfer and high-resolution tone mapping, with the latter being an inverse process that reverts the applied tone. The proposed approach achieves impressive accuracy, with a normalized mean squared error of 0.030 on our own dataset and 0.048 on OpenCV's halton tone generator.

We present the LOW-POLY 3D Object Detection challenge, focusing on highly optimized 3D object detection models for efficient processing. Our approach utilizes low-poly representations of both points and vehicles to reduce computational requirements by lowering memory and floating-point operations. A novel technical paper outlines the specific format required for data annotation, as well as a simplified point cloud model and camera intrinsics. We invite participants to utilize our provided dataset and benchmarking tools, as well as contribute their own research to the area of lightweight 3D object detection.

The number of snowflakes at the surface of the atmosphere below a specific height at any given location can vary significantly, ranging from a lack of snow to intense snowfall within a short distance. This discrepancy arises because of the complex dynamics governing snow accumulation, the process that leads to a high number of snowflakes at the surface with very little snowfall just above it. An old theory attempts to explain this phenomenon by citing a specific level of atmospheric turbulence, but our research presents an alternative explanation based on a more fundamental principle. According to our findings, the presence of numerous snowflakes at the surface is due to a preferential concentration effect where turbulent movements cause snowflakes to gather in the same area, rather than a distinct boundary layer at that height.
